q: What rule governs interaction between magnetic poles?
a: Like poles repel; opposite poles attract (N-S attracts, N-N repels).

q: In which direction does a freely suspended bar magnet settle?
Differentiate between magnetic and non-magnetic materials with examples.
a: Magnetic materials are attracted by magnets (e.g., Iron, Steel, Nickel, Cobalt). Non-magnetic materials are not attracted (e.g., Wood, Plastic, Glass, Rubber, Copper).

q: Where is the magnetic force strongest in a bar magnet?
a: At the two ends known as the magnetic poles (North Pole and South Pole).

q: How can an unmagnetized iron sewing needle be magnetized using the single-touch method?
a: Stroke the needle repeatedly (30–40 times) in one direction along its length using one fixed pole of a bar magnet, lifting the magnet clear between strokes.

q: Why is magnetic repulsion considered the only sure test for confirming whether an object is a magnet?
a: Because a magnet can attract both opposite magnetic poles and unmagnetized magnetic materials (like soft iron), but repulsion occurs exclusively between like poles of two magnets.

q: What physical actions cause a magnet to lose its magnetic properties?
a: Heating to high temperatures, hammering, or dropping from heights onto hard surfaces.
